title: Hurricane Preparedness Checklist for Texas Renters and Homeowners
seo_title: Hurricane Preparedness Checklist for Texas Homes & Rentals
meta_description: A hurricane preparedness checklist for Texas: build a go-kit, protect documents, know your zone, secure your home and stay safe after.
body_html:
If you live anywhere from Brownsville to Beaumont, or a few hours inland, hurricane season is part of the deal. The good news: most of what keeps you safe can be done on a calm weekend in May or June, long before a storm has a name. This hurricane preparedness checklist covers what Texas renters and homeowners actually need to do before, during and after a storm.

When to start: Texas hurricane season basics

Atlantic hurricane season runs from June 1 through November 30, and the busiest stretch usually falls between mid-August and October. Storms can strengthen quickly over the warm Gulf, so the gap between "something is forming" and "it's at our door" can be just a few days.

That's why the smartest move is to prep early, while stores are stocked and you aren't fighting for the last case of water. Bookmark the National Hurricane Center for official forecasts, and follow your local National Weather Service office and county emergency management on the channels you actually check.

Hurricanes aren't only a coastal problem. Heavy rain and flooding can reach far inland, and tornadoes can spin up in a storm's outer bands. If you're not sure how your area's weather risks stack up, our Texas climate regions guide breaks it down.

Build your hurricane go-kit

A go-kit is a grab-and-go bag, or a couple of bins, holding everything your household needs for at least several days without power, running water or open stores. Pack it once, store it somewhere easy to reach, and check it every spring.

  • Water: at least one gallon per person per day for several days. Add more for pets and for Texas heat.
  • Food: shelf-stable items you'll actually eat, plus a manual can opener.
  • Light and power: flashlights, extra batteries, charged power banks, and a battery or hand-crank weather radio.
  • First aid: a basic kit, plus a supply of prescription medications if you can get one.
  • Hygiene: wipes, hand sanitizer, toilet paper, trash bags and feminine products.
  • Cash: small bills. Card readers and ATMs go down when the power does.
  • Pet supplies: food, water, a leash or carrier, vaccination records and a recent photo.
  • Personal items: a change of clothes, sturdy closed-toe shoes, spare glasses, chargers, and something to keep kids busy.

During the season, try to keep your car's gas tank at least half full. Lines get long before a storm, and pumps need power too.

Protect your important documents

After a storm, you may need to prove who you are, where you live and what you owned. Gather these into a waterproof pouch or document bag that lives with your go-kit:

  • Driver's licenses, passports and Social Security cards
  • Your lease, or your mortgage paperwork and deed
  • Insurance policies (renters, homeowners, flood, auto) with policy numbers and claims phone numbers
  • Medical information, prescription lists and pet vaccination records
  • A written list of emergency contacts, in case your phone dies

Then back everything up digitally by scanning or photographing documents into a secure cloud folder. While you're at it, walk through your home and video every room, opening closets and drawers as you go. That footage makes an insurance claim much easier. Renters, our guide to filing a renters storm damage claim explains what adjusters typically ask for.

Know your zone and your evacuation plan

Many Texas coastal communities use evacuation zones, often organized by ZIP code, so officials can order specific areas to leave in stages. Look up your zone on your county or city emergency management website before the season starts, and write it down where everyone in the house can see it.

  • If you're in an evacuation zone: leave when officials tell you to. Storm surge, not wind, is often the deadliest part of a hurricane.
  • If you're not in a zone: sheltering at home may be safer than sitting in evacuation traffic, unless officials advise otherwise, your home is unsafe or flood-prone, or you rely on power for medical equipment.
  • Pick a destination: a friend or relative inland, a hotel booked early, or a public shelter. Confirm whether it accepts pets.
  • Map two routes and keep a paper map in the car in case cell service drops.
  • Need help evacuating? Texas runs the State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry (STEAR) for people who may need extra help during a disaster. Dial 2-1-1 to learn more or register.

Ready.gov's hurricane page is a good place to turn this into a written family plan.

Securing a rental vs. securing a house

What you can do, and what you're expected to do, depends on whether you own the place.

If you rent

  • Read your lease for storm-related rules, and ask management what they'll handle, such as shutters, boarding windows, or moving cars out of flood-prone lots.
  • Bring everything inside from your balcony or patio: furniture, grills, plants and decor. Loose items become projectiles in high wind.
  • Don't drill into walls or window frames without written permission.
  • Check your renters insurance. It covers your belongings, not the building, and standard policies usually exclude flood. Separate flood coverage for contents is available to renters, but new policies often have a waiting period before they kick in, so don't wait for a forecast.
  • Move electronics and valuables up off the floor, especially in a ground-floor unit.

If you own

  • Protect windows with storm shutters or pre-cut, labeled plywood. Taping windows does not keep glass from breaking.
  • Trim trees and clean gutters early in the season, not the day before landfall.
  • Secure or store patio furniture, trash cans and anything else that could blow around.
  • Review your policies. Homeowners insurance typically excludes flood. In some coastal counties, wind coverage comes through the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association (TWIA) rather than your regular policy.
  • Learn how to shut off your main water valve, electricity and gas in case officials instruct you to.

Your 72-hour storm countdown

When a storm is headed your way, work through this list:

  1. Charge phones, power banks and any portable power station.
  2. Fill your gas tank and pick up cash.
  3. Refill prescriptions.
  4. Freeze water bottles or containers to help keep the fridge cold longer.
  5. Turn your fridge and freezer to their coldest settings.
  6. Bring in or tie down everything outside.
  7. Fill clean containers with drinking water, and fill the bathtub for flushing and cleaning.
  8. Confirm your route and destination, and share your plan with family.

If the lights go out, our guide on what to do during a power outage covers food safety and staying cool.

After the storm: stay safe and start recovering

The danger doesn't end when the wind dies down. Plenty of storm-related injuries happen during cleanup.

  • Wait for the all-clear before returning home if you evacuated.
  • Turn around, don't drown. Never drive or walk through floodwater. It can be deeper than it looks, hide debris or downed lines, and just a few inches of moving water can knock you off your feet.
  • Stay away from downed power lines and report them to your utility.
  • Run generators outdoors only. Never use a generator, charcoal grill or camp stove inside your home, garage or carport, even with the door open. Carbon monoxide is odorless and can kill quickly. Keep generators well away from doors, windows and vents, and use battery-powered CO alarms.
  • Document damage with photos and video before you clean up, and keep receipts for repairs, supplies and hotel stays.
  • Renters: tell your landlord about damage in writing right away, and contact your insurer about your belongings.
  • When in doubt, throw it out. Toss perishable food that sat above 40°F for more than two hours, and anything that touched floodwater.
  • Watch for mold. Dry wet areas within 24 to 48 hours if you can, and wear gloves and an N95 respirator when cleaning moldy spots. Large areas or sewage-contaminated water call for professionals.

Frequently asked questions

How much water do I need for a hurricane?

Plan on at least one gallon per person per day for several days, plus extra for pets. Many Texans keep enough for a week or more, since water service can be disrupted after a major storm.

Does renters insurance cover hurricane damage?

It often covers wind damage to your belongings, but standard renters policies usually exclude flooding. Read your policy and consider separate flood coverage for your contents.

Should I evacuate if I'm not in an evacuation zone?

Usually you can shelter in place if your home is sturdy and not prone to flooding. Leave if officials advise it, your home is unsafe, or you depend on electricity for medical needs.

When should I start preparing?

Ideally before June 1. Build your kit, check your insurance and look up your zone early, so when a storm forms you're only topping off supplies.
